extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, lawgivers, and students of political theory
extracted.subtask_short: preserving governments and causes of revolution
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for diagnosing why different forms of government (democracy, oligarchy, aristocracy, monarchy/tyranny) are liable to revolution and practical measures to preserve or reform constitutions. Aimed at lawmakers and political practitioners to design institutions and customs that maintain stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedition arises when opposing parts approach equality
rubrics_metrics.description: A state is liable to commotions when those parts of it which seem to be opposite to each other approach to an equality, as the rich and the common people; so that the part which is between them both is either nothing at all, or too little to be noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one party is evidently stronger the other will not risk danger; when the middle part is too small there is insufficient stabilising influence. Monitor the size and influence of intermediary groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions are brought about by violence or fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions therein are brought about in two ways, either by violence or fraud: if by violence, either at first by compelling them to submit to the change when it is made. It may also be brought about by fraud in two different ways, either when the people, being at first deceived, willingly consent to an alteration in their government, and are afterwards obliged by force to abide by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch both overt force and deceptive popular consent (examples: the four hundred using false pretence about Persian money). Prevent both military coups and fraudulent manipulation of consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demagogues destabilise democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracies will be most subject to revolutions from the dishonesty of their demagogues; for partly, by informing against men of property, they induce them to join together through self-defence, ... and partly by setting the common people against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against leaders who curry favour with the masses by attacking property-holders or by manipulative accusations; examples provided: Cos, Rhodes, Heraclea, Megara.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demagogues use bribery and obstruction to create crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Demagogues, by distributing of bribes, prevent the people from paying the trierarchs what was owing to them, who were obliged by the number of actions they were harassed with to conspire together and destroy the popular state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent corrupt distribution of public funds and manipulative withholding of obligations that generate class alliances against the regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military demagogues historically become tyrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Formerly, when the same person was both demagogue and general, the democracies were changed into tyrannies; ... because at that time the demagogues were of the soldiery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid concentrating military command and popular rhetorical influence in the same individual; separate military leadership from popular demagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a census or poor electoral regulation can alter democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: A government shall also alter from its ancient and approved democratic form into one entirely new, if there is no census to regulate the election of magistrates; for, as the election is with the people, the demagogues who are desirous of being in office, to flatter them, will endeavour with all their power to make the people superior even to the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutional mechanisms (e.g., tribal election, census rules) to restrain opportunistic demagogues; prefer election by tribes rather than wholesale popular votes if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchies perish when the people are ill-used
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two things which of all others most evidently occasion a revolution in an oligarchy; one is, when the people are ill used, for then every individual is ripe for sedition; more particularly if one of the oligarchy should happen to be their leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent oppression of non-governing classes; be attentive to popular grievances that can be rallied by a leader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluding large groups from administration invites revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a revolution is brought about by the rich who have no share in the administration, which is in the hands of a very few indeed: ... those who had no share in the government ceased not to raise disputes till they were admitted to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure avenues of access to power for significant social groups (e.g., elder brothers then younger) to prevent persistent aggrievement and insurgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal quarrels among ruling few destabilise oligarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: An oligarchy is also subject to revolutions from those who are in office therein, from the quarrels of the demagogues with each other. ... when some desire to contract the power of the oligarchy into fewer hands; for those who endeavour to support an equality are obliged to apply to the people for assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create institutional conflict-resolution among elites and guard against factional concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two sorts of demagogues in oligarchies create instability
rubrics_metrics.description: The demagogues are of two sorts; one who flatter the few when they are in power ... The others are those demagogues who have a share in the oligarchy, and flatter the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and counter both elites' clientelists and populist elites who court the masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on mercenaries and their commanders risks tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: An oligarchy is also subject to revolutions when they create another oligarchy under it; ... in war, because through a distrust in the citizens the government is obliged to employ mercenary troops, and he to whom they give the command of the army will very often assume the tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer citizen militias to mercenaries or ensure strict controls on commanders to prevent them becoming kingmakers or usurpers (example: Timophanes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating nested oligarchies (senates for life) undermines stability
rubrics_metrics.description: An oligarchy will be destroyed when they create another oligarchy under it; that is, when the management of public affairs is in the hands of a few, and not equally, but when all of them do not partake of the supreme power, as happened once at Elis ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lifetime closed senates and selection procedures that preserve power within families; broaden access to governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracies fail when virtue is not joined to power or when mixture is wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Free states and aristocracies are mostly destroyed from want of a fixed administration of public affairs; the cause of which evil arises at first from want of a due mixture of the democratic and the oligarchic parts in a free state; and in an aristocracy from the same causes, and also from virtue not being properly joined to power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend democratic and oligarchic elements suitably; ensure that those in power possess appropriate virtue and capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption begins with small illegalities; guard the first offence
rubrics_metrics.description: In well-tempered governments it requires as much care as anything whatsoever, that nothing be done contrary to law: and this ought chiefly to be attended to in matters of small consequence; for an illegality that approaches insensibly, approaches secretly ... small expenses continually repeated consume a man's income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent and correct minor illegal practices early; legislate against incremental erosions of law and custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discredit deceptive popular leaders — do not give credit to deceivers
rubrics_metrics.description: No credit ought to be given to those who endeavour to deceive the people with false pretences; for they will be confuted by facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose false pretences with facts; limit the influence of manipulators who promise unrealistic remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-officeholders among magistrates and avoid injuring aspirants
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocracies and oligarchies continuing firm ... from the wise conduct of the magistrates, both towards those who have a part in the management of public affairs, and those also who have not: towards those who have not, by never injuring them; and also introducing those who are of most consequence amongst them into office; nor disgracing those who are desirous of honour; or encroaching on the property of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inclusion, appointment, and protection of property to reduce resentment; integrate prominent non-officeholders into governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotate office and limit tenure to prevent corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: If the administration is in the hands of many, those rules which are established in democracies will be very useful; as to let no one continue in office longer than six months: that all those who are of the same rank may have their turn; ... it is from hence that tyrannies arise in democracies and oligarchies; for either those who are most powerful in each state establish a tyranny ... or the chief magistrates who have been long in power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish short tenures and systematic rotation so no individual accumulates excessive influence over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use perceived threats to keep civic vigilance high
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have the guardianship of the constitution to be able to awaken the fears of the people, that they may preserve it, and not like a night-guard to be remiss in protecting the state, but to make the distant danger appear at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ prudent rhetoric and institutions to sustain attention to external threats that justify constitutional vigilance (without abusing fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain noble quarrels by law and prevent their spread
rubrics_metrics.description: Great care ought also to be used to endeavour to restrain the quarrels and disputes of the nobles by laws, as well as to prevent those who are not already engaged in them from taking a part therein; for to perceive an evil at its very first approach is not the lot of every one, but of the politician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislate dispute-resolution among elites and limit elite conflicts that can expand into broader sedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularly adjust the census to reflect total wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent any alteration taking place in an oligarchy or free state on account of the census ... it will be useful to take a general account of the whole amount of it in former times, to compare it with the present, and to do this every year in those cities where the census is yearly ... in larger communities once in three or five years; and if the whole should be found much larger or much less than it was at the time when the census was first established ... let there be a law either to extend or contract it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institute periodic financial audits and legally mandated census adjustments to avoid unintended broadening or narrowing of eligibility for office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent anyone from acquiring rank far superior to others
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a general maxim in democracies, oligarchies, monarchies, and indeed in all governments, not to let any one acquire a rank far superior to the rest of the community, but rather to endeavour to confer moderate honours for a continuance than great ones for a short time; for these latter spoil men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer modest, long-term honors rather than sudden great promotions; legislate limits on concentrations of rank, wealth, and patronage; if removing honors, do so gradually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint officers to inspect manners and guard the state's character
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be a particular officer to inspect the manners of every one, and see that these are not contrary to the genius of the state in which he lives, whether it may be an oligarchy, a democracy, or any other form of government; and, for the same reason, those should be guarded against who are most prosperous in the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create cultural oversight or civic education officers who monitor conduct and curb innovations that subvert constitutional character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend rich and poor; grow the middle rank
rubrics_metrics.description: I mean, to oppose men of account to the common people, the poor to the rich, and to blend both these into one body, and to increase the numbers of those who are in the middle rank; and this will prevent those seditions which arise from an inequality of condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enact policies that enlarge and empower middle ranks (social mobility, mixed recruitment to offices) to stabilise society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent venality of public officers, especially in oligarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all, in every state it is necessary, both by the laws and every other method possible, to prevent those who are employed by the public from being venal, and this particularly in an oligarchy; for then the people will not be so much displeased ... as at suspecting that the officers of the state steal the public money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institute anti-corruption measures, audits, and severe sanctions for embezzlement to reduce public resentment and loss of legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make public office unpaid to balance aristocracy and democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one method of blending together a democracy and an aristocracy, if office brought no profit; by which means both the rich and the poor will enjoy what they desire; for to admit all to a share in the government is democratical; that the rich should be in office is aristocratical. This must be done by letting no public employment whatsoever be attended with any emolument; for the poor will not desire to be in office when they can get nothing by it, but had rather attend to their own affairs: but the rich will choose it, as they want nothing of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove monetary emoluments from offices; instead provide honourific rewards so that poor citizens are less tempted by office for gain while the wealthy still serve for prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in public finance and open accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent the exchequer from being defrauded, let all public money be delivered out openly in the face of the whole city, and let copies of the accounts be deposited in the different wards tribes, and divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish and distribute financial records widely; hold open distributions/audits to prevent embezzlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect property of the rich in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies also it is necessary that the rich should be protected, by not permitting their lands to be divided, nor even the produce of them, which in some states is done unperceivably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against stealthy expropriation or subdivision practices; discourage extravagant public entertainments that drain wealthy citizens and generate resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide gainful public employment to the poor in oligarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: In an oligarchy it is necessary to take great care of the poor, and allot them public employments which are gainful; and, if any of the rich insult them, to let their punishment be severer than if they insulted one of their own rank; and to let estates pass by affinity, and not gift: nor to permit any person to have more than one; for by this means property will be more equally divided, and the greater part of the poor get into better circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public employment, harsher penalties for elite insults to lower ranks, inheritance rules (pass by affinity not gifts), and limits on estate accumulation to reduce inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill principal offices with those best qualified
rubrics_metrics.description: Still all the principal offices in the state to be filled only by those who are best qualified to discharge them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise competence in appointments regardless of regime type; meritocratic selection for key functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three qualifications for top officials
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three qualifications necessary for those who fill the first departments in government; first of all, an affection for the established constitution; second place, abilities every way completely equal to the business of their office; in the third, virtue and justice correspondent to the nature of that particular state they are placed in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek officeholders who love the constitution, possess requisite ability, and exhibit state-appropriate virtue; weigh tradeoffs when not all three are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer different qualities depending on office (trade-offs in selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the choice of a general we should regard his courage more than his virtue ... but, to protect the state or manage the finances, the contrary rule should be followed; for these require greater virtue ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor selection criteria to office function: valor for military command, virtue and probity for finance and civil protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of children to the constitution preserves the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all things which I have mentioned, that which contributes most to preserve the state is, what is now most despised, to educate your children for the state; ... the citizens are not accustomed to and brought up in the principles of the constitution; of a democracy, if that is by law established; of an oligarchy, if that is; for if there are bad morals in one man, there are in the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement civic education that inculcates constitutional principles across classes; avoid raising magistrates' children in ways that promote class resentment or innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the mean; avoid extremes in constitutional practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all things that ought not to be forgotten ... namely, to preserve a mean. For many things seemingly favourable to a democracy destroy a democracy, and many things seemingly favourable to an oligarchy destroy an oligarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extreme implementations of any regime's values; seek balanced, mixed institutions and guard against excessive extension of any single principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demagogues must not make the people superior to the laws
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also an error in democracies for the demagogues to endeavour to make the common people superior to the laws; and thus by setting them at variance with the rich ... whereas they ought rather to speak in favour of the rich.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent charismatic leaders from undermining rule of law by flattering popular passions; maintain legal primacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oaths in oligarchy should declare non-injury to the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The oaths also which they take in an oligarchy ought to be contrary to what they now are; for, at present, in some places they swear, 'I will be adverse to the common people, and contrive all I can against them;' whereas they ought rather to suppose and pretend the contrary; expressing in their oaths, that they will not injure the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design public oaths and pledges to affirm duty to the whole community, reducing institutional hostility to non-elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy vs Tyranny: ends and guards differ
rubrics_metrics.description: A kingdom partakes much of the nature of an aristocracy ... A king desires to be the guardian of his people, that those who have property may be secure in the possession of it, and that the people in general meet with no injury; but a tyrant ... has no regard to the common good, except for his own advantage; his only object is pleasure, but a king's is virtue: what a tyrant therefore is ambitious of engrossing is wealth, but a king rather honour. The guards too of a king are citizens, a tyrant's foreigners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate institutional design for monarchies (promote civic guards, honor-based legitimacy) from tyrannies (whose features to avoid: foreign guards, personal enrichment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchies dissolve from injustice, contempt, and dispossession
rubrics_metrics.description: Through injustice received, fear, and contempt, many of those who are under a monarchical government conspire against it; but of all species of injustice, injurious contempt has most influence on them for that purpose: sometimes it is owing to their being deprived of their private fortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent contempt and economic dispossession under monarchies; safeguard private property and dignity to reduce conspiratorial pressures.
